analysis.one_liner: Establishes a federal right to abortion care, blocking state bans, waiting periods, and provider-targeted restrictions.
analysis.headline: The Senate voted 49-51 on May 11, 2022, falling 11 votes short of the 60 needed to open debate, with every Republican and one Democrat opposed, and the bill never advanced.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a federal statutory right for patients to get abortions and for providers to perform them. Governments could not ban abortion before fetal viability, force medically unnecessary in-person visits or counseling, restrict medication abortion or telemedicine, or impose rules on abortion providers that don't apply to doctors doing comparable procedures. It would override existing state restrictions and let the Justice Department, patients, and providers sue to enforce it. The Senate never got to debate it: a procedural vote requiring 60 senators failed 49-51.
analysis.who_benefits: People seeking abortions — especially low-income women in states that ban or heavily restrict the procedure, who would otherwise have to travel out of state, take time off work, and pay for child care and travel. Providers also gain a statutory right to offer abortion care without targeted state rules, plus a private right of action with attorney's fees to fight restrictions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women seeking abortions, especially in restrictive states

how_it_helps.text: Guarantees a statutory right for providers to offer abortion services and patients to receive them, and bans government prohibition of abortion before fetal viability or after viability when the provider judges the pregnancy risks the patient's life or health.

Eliminates common state restrictions such as mandatory waiting periods requiring extra in-person trips, counseling scripts with medically inaccurate information, and facility, staffing, or credentialing rules not imposed on doctors performing medically comparable procedures.
Protects access to medication abortion under current evidence-based regimens and to abortion via telemedicine, except for limits that apply to telemedicine generally.

Gives the Justice Department, patients, and providers the power to sue states and officials, strips state immunity from such suits, applies to restrictions enacted before passage, and awards court costs and attorney's fees to winning plaintiffs.

analysis.who_pays: State governments that restrict abortion would lose the power to enforce those laws — including bans enacted before the bill's passage — and would face federal lawsuits from the Justice Department, providers, and patients. States would also bear the cost of litigating whether their rules meet the bill's strict safety justification standard.

drawbacks.text: The bill goes beyond codifying the previous constitutional framework: it bars any ban before viability, defines viability by the treating provider's judgment, and allows post-viability abortion whenever the provider judges the pregnancy risks the patient's health, so states could set no gestational limits at all.

Its catch-all provision blocks any state measure that 'singles out' abortion and impedes access unless the state proves by clear and convincing evidence that the rule significantly advances patient safety and no less restrictive alternative exists — a standard that would sweep away popular state rules like waiting periods and informed-consent laws along with bans.
The bill expressly does not apply to insurance or Medicaid coverage of abortion, so it guarantees a legal right to the procedure but does nothing about its cost for people who cannot afford it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people in states with bans or waiting periods, the bill would restore access they lost and remove barriers that fall hardest on low-income women, and its enforcement tools are unusually strong. The honest cost is breadth: the same bill that would strike down bans would also strike down state regulations many voters support, and it leaves affordability untouched because insurance coverage is carved out. As drafted, that breadth helped limit its coalition to 49 votes when 60 were needed.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate failed a procedural vote that needed 60 senators to even start debate, 49-51, so the bill never got a floor vote and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill on May 3, 2022, and it was placed on the Senate calendar within a day.

On May 11, 2022, a cloture motion — a procedural vote needing 60 senators just to begin debate — failed 49 to 51: all 50 Republicans and Democrat Joe Manchin voted no, while 47 Democrats and both independents voted yes.
With no further action taken, the bill died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments that restrict abortion and opponents of the bill — the existing patchwork of state abortion laws stayed fully in force because the bill never reached the floor.

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and brought it to the floor for a test vote five weeks after the draft opinion overturning Roe v. Wade leaked.

for.name: 47 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on cloture, the procedural vote to begin debate.

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on cloture unanimously, denying the 60 votes needed to begin debate.

against.name: Joe Manchin
against.what_they_did: Cast the only Democratic vote against cloture.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split almost entirely by party: all 50 Republicans plus one Democrat voted no, while 47 of 48 Democrats and both independents voted yes — 49 for, 51 against.

industries.note: The bill gives providers a statutory right to offer abortion care free of state rules that single them out, plus the ability to sue states with attorney's fees awarded to prevailing plaintiffs. Patients gain access to the same services, so the industry's interest in this bill runs alongside the public's.

The bill bars states from restricting telemedicine abortion or prescribing abortion drugs under current evidence-based regimens, expanding the channels through which people can obtain care. That expands options for patients at the same time it expands these providers' reach.
